newsitem.title: DENMARK: FOCUS-Denmark to ease fiscal reins in 1998.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Denmark to ease fiscal reins in 1998.

text.p: Danish Finance Minister Mogens Lykketoft on Tuesday said he expected fiscal tightening to ease in 1998 to around 0.25 percent of gross domestic product compared with 0.4 percent in 1997.

Local financial markets took the projections in their stride and were little affected. But the plans were unlikely to find favour with economists, many of whom have recently called for greater tightening to stave off overheating in the economy.
"We expect a slightly lower level (in 1998 than in 1997), something like a fiscal effect of minus 0.25 percent," Lykketoft told a news conference.
Economy Minister Marianne Jelved added that the net effect of the 1998 tightening would be increased by the introduction of a planned tax reform, but did not say by how much.

The proposed fiscal tightening falls short of recommendations last week by the independent advisors of the Danish Economic Council. They said the 1998 tightening should be at least four billion crowns ($620 million) -- equivalent to around 0.4 percent of GDP.
But Jelved last Wednesday said the net effect in 1998 would be sufficient.
"The government intends to tighten fiscal policy in 1998 by more than the four billion crowns mentioned in the Economic Council report," she told Reuters.
The government also updated a number of its periodic economic forecasts.
The finance ministry sharply raised its expectations for the 1997 state budget to a surplus of 4.8 billion crowns, from a December forecast of a 5.9 billion crown deficit.
"The improvement is due to increased revenues from income tax, corporation tax and value added tax," the ministry wrote in its latest budget outlook.
The economy ministry also revised its expectations from its last outlook in December 1996.
It forecast GDP growth of 3.3 percent in 1997 and 3.0 percent in 1998, up from December projections of 2.9 percent for 1997 and 2.7 percent the following year.
Unemployment was seen at 7.8 percent in 1997 and 7.4 percent in 1998, compared with the previous forecast of 8.0 percent and 7.6 percent respectively.

Export growth prospects were mixed. The ministry upgraded its expectations for 1997 growth to 4.3 percent from its former 4.1 percent but revised its 1998 prognosis down to 4.5 percent from 4.6 percent.
For imports the forecast was 4.1 percent in 1997 and 4.2 percent in 1998. The previous forecast was for 3.6 percent and 4.6 percent.
The outlook for 1997 inflation was unchanged at 2.3 percent but for 1998 consumer prices were seen rising 2.4 percent, compared with an earlier 2.3 percent prediction.
Personal consumption figures were revised upward for both years, to growth of 2.7 percent in 1997 and 3.1 percent the following year from December's 2.5 and 3.0 percent.

The current account was seen deteriorating slightly, with a 1997 surplus of 12 billion crowns, compared with the previous forecast of 13 billion, and a 1998 surplus of 13 billion crowns, down from a previous 15 billion estimate.
The public sector budget surplus was seen sharply up for both years, at seven billion crowns in 1997 and eight billion in 1998 from a previous estimate of two billion crowns and 4.8 billion.
